# Pipelining and Compiled Plans {#sec-pipelining}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A physical plan is a DAG of operators. A pipelined plan is a DAG
of *pipelines*, each pipeline being a chain of operators that the
JIT can fuse into a single tight loop. Pipelining is the engine's
answer to a question every query compiler eventually faces: where
do I draw the boundaries of the generated code?

The wrong answer in either direction is bad. Generate one giant
function for the whole plan and you waste compile time on code
that does not need to be co-optimised, and you cannot release
intermediate state until the whole query finishes. Generate one
function per operator and you incur a function-call boundary at
every record, defeating the point of code generation in the first
place.

The right answer is well known [@hyper-paper]: fuse what can be
fused (operators that pass records one-at-a-time), break at
operators that materialise (joins, aggregations, sorts). The
operators where you must break are called *pipeline breakers*.

NebulaStream's `PipeliningPhase` does exactly this.

---

## 11.1 The shape of a pipeline {#sec-pipeline-shape}

A pipeline is a sequence of physical operators with a single
producer (a source operator or a probe operator) and a single
consumer (a sink operator or a build operator). Records flow from
producer to consumer through the chain, one at a time, with no
intermediate materialisation. The JIT generates one function whose
loop body executes the chain.

The data structure is in
`nes-query-compiler/include/PipelinedQueryPlan.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/include/PipelinedQueryPlan.hpp
struct PipelinedQueryPlan final {
    explicit PipelinedQueryPlan(QueryId id, ExecutionMode executionMode);
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Pipeline>> getSourcePipelines() const;
    [[nodiscard]] const std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Pipeline>>& getPipelines() const;
    void addPipeline(const std::shared_ptr<Pipeline>& pipeline);
    void removePipeline(Pipeline& pipeline);
};
```

A `PipelinedQueryPlan` is a vector of `Pipeline`s, distinguishing
the *source pipelines* (those starting at a source operator) from
the rest. The distinction matters because source pipelines are the
ones that get scheduled when sources produce data; everything else
is reactive.

---

## 11.2 The pipelining phase {#sec-pipelining-phase}

The phase is `PipeliningPhase`, in
`nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/PipeliningPhase.hpp`. Its
algorithm, simplified:

1. Walk the physical plan in topological order.
2. For each operator, decide whether to *continue* the current
   pipeline or start a *new* pipeline.
3. The decision is encoded as `PipelinePolicy::Continue` or
   `PipelinePolicy::ForceNew`.

The enum and its case analysis live in
`nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp`:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp
enum class PipelinePolicy : uint8_t {
    Continue,   /// Uses the current pipeline for the next operator
    ForceNew    /// Enforces a new pipeline for the next operator
};
```

The recursive builder applies five rules in order; the first
match wins:

| # | Operator kind | Policy | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Custom Scan | `ForceNew` | New pipeline begins at the scan; child operators chain in |
| 2 | Custom Emit | `ForceNew` | A scan must precede an emit if the previous op was also an emit |
| 3 | Sink | `ForceNew` | Sinks are pipeline terminators; format operators may be inserted |
| 4 | Merge point (in-degree > 1) | `ForceNew` (override) | A DAG node with multiple parents cannot be fused into either parent |
| 5 | Fusible (Selection, Projection, Map) | `Continue` | Default; appended to current pipeline |

Rule 4 is the override that catches operators that *would* have
been fusible but cannot be because two upstream pipelines feed
them. The check is a single line:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp (sketch)
if (policy != PipelinePolicy::ForceNew && mergePoints.contains(opId)) {
    policy = PipelinePolicy::ForceNew;
}
```

A sink is always a pipeline breaker because the engine does not
fuse sink writes with operator computation. A stateful build
(join build, aggregation build) is a pipeline breaker because
the build materialises into a hash map. A stateful probe is the
*start* of a new pipeline, because it consumes from the
materialised state asynchronously.

The fusible operators — Selection, Projection, Map — get
`PipelinePolicy::Continue` by default and become part of
whatever pipeline they sit in.

---

## 11.3 Pipeline breakers, walked through {#sec-breakers}

For our running demo query (Chapter 2), the pipelined plan is
trivial:

```
Pipeline 1: [SourcePhysicalOperator(demo) → SinkPhysicalOperator(result)]
```

One source pipeline, one sink, no break in between (because there
is no stateful operator). The JIT generates one function for the
whole pipeline; the loop body reads a record from the source,
projects (in this case, identity), writes to the sink. Done.

For a hash-join query, the picture is more interesting. Consider:

```sql
SELECT * FROM r JOIN s ON r.key = s.key INTO matched;
```

After lowering (Chapter 10), the physical plan is:

```
Sink ← HJProbe ← Source(s)
       HJBuild ← Source(r)
```

`HJProbe` is the consumer of records from `s`; `HJBuild` is the
consumer of records from `r`. The two halves share an
`OperatorHandlerId` that points to a single hash map.

After pipelining, this becomes three pipelines:

```
Pipeline A (source pipeline): [Source(r) → HJBuild]
Pipeline B (source pipeline): [Source(s) → HJProbe → Sink]
```

`HJBuild` is a pipeline breaker; pipeline A ends at it. `HJProbe`
starts pipeline B. The two pipelines are independent at the
scheduler's level — they run as separate compiled functions, each
producing/consuming `WorkTask`s — but they communicate through the
shared hash map handler.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.1: aggregation pipelines"}
A windowed aggregation `SELECT AVG(x) FROM s GROUP BY k WINDOW
TUMBLING(ts, 1 SEC)` lowers and pipelines into:

```
Pipeline A: [Source(s) → AggregationBuild]
Pipeline B: [AggregationProbe → Sink]
```

Pipeline A executes whenever a source-emitted `WorkTask` lands.
Pipeline B executes when a window fires (driven by watermarks
from pipeline A). The hash map is owned by the aggregation
handler; pipeline A inserts, pipeline B walks and emits.
:::

---

## 11.4 Within a pipeline: the producer/consumer protocol {#sec-producer-consumer}

Inside a pipeline, the operators do not call each other through C++
methods. They communicate through the `Record` interface, which is
the per-tuple data structure the JIT operates on:

```cpp
// nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/Interface/Record.hpp
class Record {
public:
    explicit Record() = default;
    explicit Record(std::unordered_map<RecordFieldIdentifier, VarVal>&& recordFields);
    void reassignFields(const Record& other);
    const VarVal& read(const RecordFieldIdentifier& recordFieldIdentifier) const;
    void write(const RecordFieldIdentifier& recordFieldIdentifier,
               const VarVal& varVal);
    nautilus::val<uint64_t> getNumberOfFields() const;
    [[nodiscard]] bool hasField(const RecordFieldIdentifier& fieldName) const;
};
```

A `Record` is a typed bag of fields. The fields are of type
`VarVal`, which is a Nautilus-side variant of all the primitive
types in NebulaStream's data model. At code generation time, every
`Record::read` and `Record::write` is lowered to direct memory
accesses (via the `MemoryProvider` from Chapter 4); there is no
runtime hash lookup.

Within a pipeline, the producer's `execute` ends with
`consumer.execute(record)`; the consumer's `execute` reads fields
through `Record::read`, modifies through `Record::write`, and
forwards. The whole chain ends up as a single tight loop in the
generated code.

---

## 11.5 The compiled plan {#sec-compiled-plan}

After pipelining and JIT compilation, the plan becomes a
`CompiledQueryPlan`. The structure is in
`nes-executable/include/CompiledQueryPlan.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-executable/include/CompiledQueryPlan.hpp
struct CompiledQueryPlan {
    QueryId id;
    std::vector<ExecutablePipelineStage> stages;
    std::vector<SourceDescriptor> sources;
    std::vector<SinkDescriptor> sinks;
    // ...
};
```

`stages` is the JIT output: one `ExecutablePipelineStage` per
pipeline, each holding a function pointer (or, in INTERPRETER mode,
a trace to interpret). `sources` and `sinks` carry the
fully-specified descriptors from Chapter 8 — the worker constructs
its own source and sink instances from these without consulting the
coordinator.

The `CompiledQueryPlan` is the artefact handed to the query engine
in @sec-stage6-run for execution. It is the boundary between
"compile-time" and "run-time": everything to the left of it is
preparation, everything to the right is data flow.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch11-summary}

The pipelining phase converts a physical plan into a DAG of
pipelines, each pipeline being a chain of operators the JIT can
fuse into a single function. Pipeline breaks happen at sinks and
at the build half of stateful operator pairs. Within a pipeline,
operators communicate through the `Record` interface, which the
JIT lowers to direct memory accesses. Across pipelines, operators
communicate through shared operator handlers, scheduled as
independent `WorkTask`s by the runtime. The output of pipelining
plus JIT is a `CompiledQueryPlan` carrying both the executable
stages and the fully-specified source/sink descriptors needed by
the worker.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch11-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 11.1: count pipelines"}
For each query, predict and then verify the number of pipelines
in the compiled plan:

1. `SELECT * FROM s INTO sink;`
2. `SELECT * FROM s WHERE x > 0 INTO sink;`
3. `SELECT * FROM r JOIN s ON r.k = s.k INTO sink;`
4. `SELECT k, COUNT(*) FROM s GROUP BY k WINDOW TUMBLING(ts, 1 SEC) INTO sink;`

How does the count change as you add stateful operators?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 11.2: trace fusion"}
Add `NES_DEBUG` log lines at the start of every physical
operator's `execute`. Run a `SELECT * WHERE x > 0` query.
Observe that no virtual call appears between the source and the
sink — the selection's `execute` and the projection's `execute`
are inlined into one tight loop. The log lines should fire in
strict per-record order.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 11.3: examine the IR"}
Run any systest with `--worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=COMPILER`
and `mlir.dumpIR` enabled. The MLIR for a simple pipeline should
fit on one screen. Identify the loop, the field accesses, and
the call into the sink.
:::
